t: Minimum Threshold for Inversion Pairs Count
o: Count pairs i<j with nums[i] > nums[j] and nums[i]-nums[j] <= x; find the smallest integer x achieving at least k such pairs, or -1. The count f(x) is a non-decreasing step function that only changes at values x equal to some positive difference nums[i]-nums[j]; hence the optimal x is itself one of those differences (or unreachable). We binary search x over [0, maxDiff] and evaluate f(x) with a Fenwick tree: scanning j left to right, count earlier elements with value in (nums[j], nums[j]+x]. Example 2: f(8) = 6 >= 4 while f(7) = 3, so the answer is 8.
k: f(x) is monotone non-decreasing and piecewise constant, changing only at pairwise differences — binary search on x works and the found x is automatically a real difference.
Evaluate f(x) in O(n log n) with a value-compressed BIT: for each j add the count of previous values in (nums[j], nums[j]+x].

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search on threshold + BIT counting
a.i: Compress values. For a candidate x, sweep the array inserting each element into a BIT after querying how many previously inserted values lie in the half-open range (v, v+x]. Binary search the minimal x with f(x) >= k.
s: If the array is non-increasing everywhere with f(max) < k, return -1 (checked at the end).
count(x): reset BIT; for each element query range then insert; compare with k.
a.t: O(log(V) * n log n) — about 30 BIT sweeps of n elements each
a.sp: O(n) for compression and the BIT

w: Because f is a step function jumping only at genuine pairwise differences, the binary-searched integer x is guaranteed to be an attained difference — no post-adjustment needed. Pitfall: resetting the BIT between evaluations, and using 64-bit arithmetic for v + x. Follow-up: count all pairs for a specific x offline via merge-sort counting if only one evaluation were needed.
